newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour to talk tough on public sector pay.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour to talk tough on public sector pay.

text.p: The main opposition Labour party will set out a tough policy on public-sector pay this week as part of an effort to persuade voters it can be trusted to run the economy responsibly if it wins Britain's looming election.

Sunday newspapers said the party's economics spokesman, Gordon Brown, would warn Britain's six million public sector workers in a keynote speech on Monday that Labour would extend the government's four-year-old freeze on their pay.
The Sunday Telegraph said Brown will say: "Just as we will resist every other unreasonable demand on the public purse, we will resist other unreasonable public sector pay demands."

Labour has worked hard to shed the tax-and-spend reputation that analysts believe cost it the 1992 general election, and according to an opinion poll in the Sunday Times is now viewed as more economically competent than the ruling Conservatives.

Brown, who has ruthlesssly curbed Labour colleagues' spending plans, is expected to say that any pay increases would have to be met within the tough cash limits he intends to impose on every ministry.
This is essentially the government's present policy.

Although many trade union leaders are likely to bite their tongue for fear of harming Labour's election chances, the head of the powerful Transport and General Workers' Union, Bill Morris, accused Brown of preparing to "grind the workers into the dust".
"Public sector workers cannot be expected to bear the brunt of a tight fiscal policy," Morris told the Sunday Telegraph.
Brown's firm line on pay comes against a background of improving relations between Labour and business.

Labour officials say leader Tony Blair has been regularly advised by a group of leading businessmen and industrialists, including the chief executive of British Airways and the chairman of publishinbg group Pearsons.
Blair has repeatedly said he wants to end the traditional political divide in Britain that pits the Conservatives as the party of business against Labour as the party of the unions.

He would like Labour, too, to be accepted as a natural ally of business and aides says he is planning a series of high-profile meetings with business leaders culminating in March with the publication of the party's "Business Plan for Britain".

Blair will share a platform on Tuesday with the chairman of British Aerospace and General Electric Co at the launch of a new business manifesto commissioned by the Institute for Public Policy Research, a think tank with close ties to Labour.
Labour enjoys an opinion poll lead of almost 20 percentage points over Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives, who must call an election by May 22.
